alalal-c45275-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 8: whether being everywhere belongs to God alone, introducing a question on Lombard's text.

alalal-c45275-d1e113.summary: Takes up Lombard's claim that being everywhere is proper to divinity. First objection: the Posterior Analytics says the universal is of all, always and everywhere, so being everywhere is not proper to God.

alalal-c45275-d1e138.summary: Second objection: the Gloss on Psalm 147 says swiftness is everywhere. If one replies that a universal is everywhere only in its particulars, take the analogical universal of all effects reduced to the first cause; it is said of God and every creature, so it is everywhere and always.

alalal-c45275-d1e172.summary: Third objection: suppose only one substance existed; it would be in everything God is in, so omnipresence would not be proper to God.

alalal-c45275-d1e183.summary: Fourth objection: suppose only one man existed; his soul would be whole in his whole body, the only place, and so everywhere like God.

alalal-c45275-d1e199.summary: Fifth objection: a body large enough to fill the whole concavity of the world would be everywhere.

alalal-c45275-d1e212.summary: Solution: all such sophisms are resolved by noting that 'everywhere' is equivocal. A universal is everywhere as in its subjects, undivided from them; God is everywhere as distinct from all yet in all, giving place its power to contain and the located its power to fill.
claims: God's omnipresence differs in kind from the ubiquity of a universal, since God is distinct from and causes what he is in.

alalal-c45275-d1e251.summary: Reply to the single-substance case: such a substance would be in one place only, not everywhere, since there could be other places where it is not, but none where God is not. Also, it would not be whole in the whole place and in every part, as God is.
claims: Only God is necessarily in every possible place, and whole in the whole and in every part.
concepts: totus in toto et in qualibet parte

alalal-c45275-d1e280.summary: Reply to the soul case: the soul relates to the body as to matter and moveable, not as to place, so the supposition fails. Reply to the world-filling body: it would not be whole in every part of place, so the instance does not hold.
claims: The soul is in the body as form in matter, not as in place.

alalal-c45275.summary: Article 8 defends Lombard's claim that being everywhere is proper to God alone. Objections propose rival ubiquities: the universal, especially the analogical universal predicated of God and creatures; a sole existing substance; the soul of a sole man; and a body filling the cosmos. Albert resolves them through the equivocity of 'everywhere'. A universal is everywhere only as in its subjects, undivided from them, whereas God, distinct from all, is in all as giving place its containing power and the located its power to fill. A sole substance would not be in every possible place, nor whole in every part. The soul is in the body as form, not as in place, and a cosmic body is not whole in each part.
claims: Being everywhere is proper to God alone.
A universal is everywhere only in its subjects, while God is everywhere as a distinct cause present to all.
Only God is whole in the whole and in every part of every possible place.
